blocks.text: This is very much to the point. For idols are said to be cast to the moles and the bats when they are thrust down, as it were into darkness, from the lofty place in which they stood out, so that they may no longer deceive superstitious people with their splendour. And among the Hebrews there seems [col. 1033] to have been a proverbial expression by which something utterly despised and held in the greatest contempt was said to be cast to the moles and the bats. Accordingly Kimchi rightly holds that this is said דרך בזיון, that is, by way of contempt. Although the Patriarch Jacob also fulfilled it literally when he buried the idols of his household under the terebinth, Gen. XXXV, 4. Jerome renders it otherwise: In that day a man shall cast away the idols, etc. which he had made for himself to worship, moles and bats. So also, among the Hebrews, Rabbi Solomon. This pleases me less, although the Hebrew could bear it, because I have nowhere read that moles and bats were worshipped as gods by the ancients.
Who does not know, Bithynian Volusius, what monsters mad Egypt worships? — — —

Yet not even in Egypt did the insane frenzy of the idolaters descend so far. Though the nearest thing to it is that the Athribites worshipped the μυγάλην [mygalēn], that is, the shrew-mouse, as Strabo testifies in book 7. Not to mention the Musorites, heretical Christians, by whom shrews are read in Philastrius to have been worshipped ^{(7)}.

[II, 451] Among the works of Jerome there is extant a Book of Names, begun by Philo, enlarged by Origen, and completed by Jerome, in which are explained all the proper names that occur in the books of the Prophets. Among these you may see פרפר Farfar, the name of a river of Damascus, 2 Reg. V, 12., explained as mole; the author of this explanation, whoever he is, thought that פרפר had been shortened from the preceding חפרפר. In the same way in the Talmud a ditch is called פירה by aphaeresis for חפירא.
